A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
tangible
Real and noticeable rather than merely possible.
misappropriated
Wrongfully used money entrusted for a purpose.
preliminary
Coming before a fuller examination.
unconditional
Without limitations or exceptions.
corroborated
Supported by independent evidence.
evidential strand
A separate line of information or proof.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Sarah's call brought the first tangible consequence of Emma's decision to invite voluntary testimony. The editor had approved a restrained public notice seeking first-hand knowledge of the Glenarraidh Education Trust's 2011 student travel scheme. It would be published that afternoon, without implying that selection had been unfair, funds misappropriated or appeals deliberately obstructed.

Emma examined the approved copy for unintended assumptions. Readers were invited to describe applications they had made or assisted with, notices they had received and any information they had been given about the review procedure. Contacting the newspaper did not constitute consent to publication. Nor could the newsroom responsibly promise anonymity without first explaining its practical and legal limits.

When the notice appeared at two o'clock, Emma preserved the text and timestamp. She resisted checking for responses every few minutes. The archive still held only restricted descriptions of correspondence; Fiona's inventory had not established the contents of the unopened appeals folder. A public invitation was a method of finding evidence, not evidence in itself.

Shortly after four, Sarah forwarded a brief email from someone claiming to have assisted a student with an application in 2011. The correspondent was prepared to speak but asked not to be identified publicly. No name or supporting record in the message had yet been independently verified.

“Finally,” Sarah said. “Someone who knows what happened.”

“Someone who says they were involved,” Emma corrected. “That may prove invaluable. It isn't yet a verified account.”

Emma replied without leading questions. She proposed a confidential preliminary conversation and invited the person, if comfortable, to describe the nature of their involvement and any contemporaneous documents they retained. She distinguished a private discussion from an agreement to use quotations or identifying details in print. She also declined to offer an unconditional guarantee that no circumstances could require disclosure.

An hour later, the correspondent said they still possessed a completed application form and a letter, although they needed to decide what could appropriately be shared. Their reply gave no outcome: it did not say whether the student was selected, received money or requested reconsideration.

Emma could feel the old narrative machinery beginning to work. A preserved letter sounded like the document she had been seeking. Yet its content might be an acknowledgement, an enquiry or a final decision. Nor was there any reason to equate this person with the anonymous September parent or the author of the October item indexed by the newspaper. These were separate evidential strands until a connection could be corroborated.

The correspondent's next message proposed a conversation the following day, on the condition that recording would not begin before they had discussed consent. Emma agreed and prepared a careful interview plan: verify the person's relationship to the application, distinguish recalled events from surviving documents, agree the terms of any recording and check significant dates against independent sources.

She put the plan beside the dispatch register and the blank appeal template. The possible witness might illuminate what an administrative process felt like to someone subject to it. That perspective mattered, but it would not by itself settle every question about the trust's practices.

Emma wrote Consent at the top of a fresh page. Tomorrow she would hear a person rather than an index entry. Tonight she would make no claim about what the person was going to say.
